### Project Name Open Tool Specification (OTS) ### Project Description The OpenTool Specification (OTS) is a declarative, language-agnostic, contract-first specification for describing the capabilities that AI agents consume over the Model Context Protocol (MCP): tools, resources and prompts. OTS does for MCP capabilities what OpenAPI does for REST endpoints: a single document that a person or a machine can read to know what each capability does, which schemas it accepts and returns, which security it requires, and which backend implements it. OTS separates three concerns that today usually remain coupled: what capability is offered (the semantic interface the agent sees), how it is discovered (a unified, filtered catalog), and where and how it is executed (the concrete MCP server, database or mock that answers the call). The project has three parts: - The specification (OTS 1.0.0): top-level info, servers, security, tools, resources, prompts and components (shared schemas and security schemes). Per-capability fields include input/output schemas, backend name and argument mapping, per-tool scopes, cache TTL, idempotency, error semantics for agents, field-level output masking (x-ots-mask) and executable example scenarios, including failure cases. - The OTS Gateway, the reference implementation: a single Go binary that reads OTS documents and sits between agents and MCP servers. It returns one aggregated catalog filtered by the caller's identity, scopes and subscription; authorizes tool by tool; applies rate limits, quotas and token budgets; validates arguments and outputs; masks sensitive fields before they reach the model; routes each call to the right backend handling that backend's own credentials; and records the full trace. It supports the three MCP primitives and the MCP protocol revisions 2025-06-18, 2025-11-25 and 2026-07-28. - The OTS Visual Designer, a VS Code extension published in the Microsoft Marketplace, with a visual map of the specification, an embedded gateway, a live execution map and an integrated debugger with test cases. Why it is valuable: as organizations deploy many MCP servers, agents must discover and connect to each one individually, which causes context bloat, extra latency and token cost, scattered credentials and no single point for authorization or audit. Existing approaches (RAG-based tool retrieval, supervisor/router agent hierarchies, framework-level tool binding) each solve part of the problem but do not provide a common, implementation-independent catalog with centralized governance. OTS also enables a design-first workflow: because the contract carries example scenarios, tools can be mocked and tested before their backends exist. Origin and history: OTS was created by Pablo D. Sagarna, drawing on enterprise API management and architecture experience. The design and its rationale were published in the paper "The OpenTool Specification: A Contract-First Governance Layer for Tools, Resources and Prompts of AI Agents" (28 September 2026). The specification, gateway binaries (version 1.0.0 for macOS, Linux, Windows and FreeBSD) and examples are published under Apache 2.0. ### Preferred Lifecycle Stage (if known) Sandbox ### Alignment with AAIF Mission The AAIF exists to provide a neutral home for open, interoperable standards and tooling for agentic AI. OTS is an open, vendor-neutral contract layer built directly on top of MCP, the AAIF's anchor protocol. It addresses a problem that appears as soon as MCP is adopted at scale inside an organization: how agents discover, access and are governed across many MCP servers in a consistent and secure way. OTS contributes to the mission in three ways: interoperability (a standard, machine-readable description of MCP capabilities that any gateway, registry, IDE or agent runtime can implement); security and governance (per-capability scopes, output masking, quotas and auditability defined in the contract rather than scattered across agents); and efficiency (a single, filtered discovery operation that reduces context bloat and token consumption). Neutral governance under the AAIF is important for a specification of this kind, since its value depends on being implemented by multiple, independent vendors rather than tied to one product. ### Relation to Existing AAIF Projects Model Context Protocol (MCP): OTS is complementary to MCP and does not replace or fork it. OTS documents describe MCP tools, resources and prompts using MCP-compatible JSON Schema, and the OTS Gateway speaks standard MCP to both agents and backend servers. OTS adds a contract and governance layer above MCP, much as OpenAPI sits above HTTP. Some OTS ideas (for example, aggregated discovery, per-tool authorization metadata or output masking hints) could be offered as input to MCP specification discussions or working groups. Goose and other MCP clients: any MCP-capable agent, including goose, can consume an OTS Gateway as a single MCP endpoint without modification, gaining a unified, permission-filtered catalog instead of configuring each server individually. AGENTS.md: both projects share a philosophy of declarative, human- and machine-readable contracts for agents. AGENTS.md describes repository context for coding agents; OTS describes the external capabilities agents may use and the rules that govern them. AAIF working groups: OTS is directly relevant to the Security and Privacy, and Observability and Traceability working groups (per-capability scopes, PII masking, end-to-end call journals). ### Example Use Cases and Evidence of Adoption Enterprise agent platforms (reference scenario: a bank): a customer-facing agent handling a mortgage request discovers, in one call to the OTS Gateway, only the tools, resources and prompts its identity is allowed to use, spread across several MCP servers (core banking, document center, prompt library). Money-moving tools require a delegated end-user scope; account identifiers are masked before reaching the model. - Governing MCP servers built on top of existing API management: the reference deployment uses WSO2 API Manager as the backend with OAuth2 client credentials, showing how OTS can govern MCP servers generated from enterprise APIs. - Design-first agent development: teams write the OTS contract first and run the gateway against the contract's own example scenarios as a mock, so agent workflows can be built and tested before the backend MCP servers exist. - Cost and context control: plans with rate limits, hourly/daily quotas and token budgets per consumer, and a single place to trace who called what. Evidence of adoption and early interest: OTS is an early-stage project. It has a working reference implementation (OTS Gateway 1.0.0 with multi-platform binaries), a published VS Code extension (OTS Visual Designer) in the Microsoft Marketplace, a public paper, and complete examples. Its relevant adoption signal at this stage is whether other gateways, registries and agent runtimes implement against the specification, which is why neutral governance is sought early. ### Technical Committee Sponsor (if identified) _No response_ ### GitHub Repository URL https://github.com/psagarna/open-tool-specification ### License Apache 2.0 ### Governance Model OTS currently follows a single-maintainer model: the project creator (Pablo D. Sagarna) reviews and merges changes to the specification, the reference gateway and the VS Code extension. On admission, the project intends to adopt the LF Minimum Viable Governance (MVG) model and the LF technical charter, with a GOVERNANCE.md describing roles (maintainers, committers, contributors), how new maintainers are added, and how specification changes are decided (proposal, public review period and lazy consensus among maintainers, with a maintainer vote as fallback). ### CI/CD & Release Workflow The OTS Gateway is a single, statically compiled Go binary with no runtime dependencies. Releases are cross-compiled for macOS (arm64, amd64), Linux (amd64, arm64, arm, 386), Windows (amd64, arm64) and FreeBSD (amd64), packaged as archives and published with a SHA256SUMS.txt file so users can verify integrity; the binary reports its build with -version. The current release is 1.0.0. The VS Code extension is packaged as a .vsix and published to the Microsoft VS Code Marketplace. The specification is versioned independently of the tooling (ots: "1.0.0" in each document). Planned: public GitHub Actions workflows for build, unit and conformance tests (validating example OTS documents and running the gateway against the mock scenarios), and automated tagged releases. Target cadence: minor releases roughly monthly during the Sandbox stage, with patch releases as needed. ### Public-Facing Contribution Process for Specifications Changes to the specification are proposed through GitHub issues and pull requests on the public repository. Substantive changes (new fields, changed semantics, new enforcement rules) start as an issue describing the motivation and proposed schema, followed by a pull request updating the specification text and examples. Each field is classified as enforced, shown or documentary, and promoting a documentary field (for example aiHints, policies or errors) to enforced requires a reference implementation in the gateway and examples. Breaking changes require a new major version of the specification. ### Publicly Accessible Issue Tracker https://github.com/psagarna/open-tool-specification/issues ### External Project Dependencies The OpenTool Specification is defined in YAML (YAML 1.2, an open specification): OTS documents describing tools, resources and prompts are written in YAML, in the same way OpenAPI documents are, and the input and output schemas within them use JSON Schema. The OTS Gateway is the component that interprets and enforces OTS documents: it loads them with a Go YAML library ([library name and license]) and applies them at runtime. The gateway’s own server configuration (ots.json: listeners, backend servers and credentials, plans, quotas and subscriptions) is written in JSON and parsed with the Go standard library (encoding/json). The gateway implements the Model Context Protocol specification (MIT license) at the protocol level and is distributed as a single static Go binary; the Go toolchain and standard library are BSD-3-Clause. The VS Code extension depends on the VS Code extension API (MIT). ### Maintainers & Contributors
Name | GitHub handle | Email | Affiliation | Role | Contribution activity -- | -- | -- | -- | -- | -- Pablo D. Sagarna | @psagarna | psagarna@gmail.com | Independent | Creator, lead maintainer | https://github.com/psagarna/open-tool-specification/commits

The project currently has one actively committing maintainer and intends to grow the contributor base by publishing contribution guidelines, labelling good first issues, inviting implementers of other gateways and registries, and seeking co-maintainers from at least one additional organization during the Sandbox period.


### Leadership Team & Decision Process Leadership team: Pablo D. Sagarna (creator and lead maintainer). Decision process: today, decisions on the specification and reference implementation are made by the lead maintainer after public discussion in GitHub issues and pull requests. Upon admission, decisions will follow the LF technical charter and MVG: lazy consensus among maintainers on pull requests, with a simple-majority maintainer vote when consensus cannot be reached, and a Technical Steering Committee formed once maintainers from more than one organization are in place. ### Lifecycle Stage Evidence Requested stage: Sandbox. Against the Sandbox acceptance criteria: - OSI-approved permissive license: Apache 2.0. - Working implementation: OTS Gateway 1.0.0 (multi-platform binaries), OTS Visual Designer VS Code extension, and complete examples (blank template and the BotiBank reference scenario). - At least one actively committing maintainer, with documented intent to grow the contributor base: see Maintainers & Contributors. - Short written thesis (intended users, Growth graduation criteria, case for importance before adoption): see the linked thesis document. The full design rationale is in the paper at https://psagarna.github.io/OTS/. Summary of the thesis: intended users are platform and architecture teams running multiple MCP servers, API-management and gateway vendors, and agent-runtime developers. Growth would be justified by production use at two or more unaffiliated organizations, at least one independent implementation of the specification beyond the reference gateway, and commits from at least two organizations. The pre-adoption case is that a neutral, implementation-independent contract for MCP capabilities is most valuable if established early, before each vendor ships an incompatible proprietary format. ### Security No OpenSSF Best Practices badge yet (planned). Current posture: release artifacts are published with SHA-256 checksums; the gateway fails at load time if a referenced credential is missing; backend secrets are referenced via environment variables rather than stored in configuration; agents never hold backend credentials; sensitive output fields can be masked (full, last4/first4, email, hash, drop) before reaching the model, trace or journal; arguments and outputs are validated against the contract on every call; and access is authorized per tool with OAuth2 scopes or API keys. ### Website URL https://psagarna.github.io/OTS/ ### Documented Governance Practices (if any) None published yet; GOVERNANCE.md and CONTRIBUTING.md will be added (see Governance Model). ### Links to Social Media Accounts _No response_ ### Trademark and accounts - [x] If the project is accepted, I agree to transfer all project trademarks and accounts to the Linux Foundation under the contribution agreement. ### Details of Existing Financial Sponsorship None ### Infrastructure Needs or Requests Standard Sandbox infrastructure: CI runners for cross-platform builds and conformance tests, and hosting for the specification website and documentation. ### Additional Information Full design paper: https://psagarna.github.io/OTS/. The project is happy to work with the MCP maintainers and relevant AAIF working groups to ensure OTS stays aligned with MCP as the protocol evolves, and to contribute ideas upstream where they belong in MCP itself. ### Application contact name(s) and email(s) Pablo D.
